subject: Google ships its best AI to defenders, not customers
bodyMarkdown:
Google released its most capable AI model on Wednesday, and neither you nor I can touch it. The unrestricted version went first to hospital security teams, telecom operators, government agencies and Google's own staff, and that choice tells you more about this industry right now than the benchmark scores do.

## What Google actually shipped

The model is Gemini 4 Argon, announced Wednesday as Google's new frontier system for software engineering, finance and legal work, and cyber defence. On DeepSWE v1.1, which scores a model on long programming jobs that take many steps rather than one answer, Google reports 77.9 per cent, the best result posted so far. Google's own comparison table runs 19 tests against OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra and Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5, and puts Argon first or tied for first on 14 of them, trailing on the other five. The number I keep looking at is the output ceiling. Argon will write up to a million **tokens** in one run, tokens being the chunks of text a model reads and writes and the unit it gets billed in, up from 64,000 before. Launch price is 2 US dollars per million tokens going in and 10 dollars coming out, rising to 4 and 20 when the introductory period ends.

## Who gets it and who waits

Argon is going out through the Fairwind Program, which Google set up to hand early access to what it calls high-priority defenders, meaning governments, hospitals and telecommunications providers. Those users get the model with its cyber restrictions stripped out, the same build Google runs internally. Google says Argon found a serious flaw in healthcare software used by hospitals worldwide that exposed personal information, and that earlier frontier models walked right past it. Paid API customers and Google AI Ultra subscribers are next in line, with no date attached. VentureBeat described it as a benchmark lead retaken in limited release. The New Stack said it more plainly: it's great, and you can't have it yet. Google also says it is taking part in the United States government's voluntary process for pre-release model access, so Washington gets a look before the people paying for the API do.

## Today OpenAI starts demoting people

OpenAI runs the same idea from the other end. Its Trusted Access for Cyber program lets vetted security researchers reach Daybreak, its strongest cyber model, and as of today, October 1, existing individual members have to switch on Advanced Account Security with a hardware-backed passkey, a physical FIDO2 key you plug in and tap, or they drop back to standard model access. ChatGPT still works for them. The capable model does not. Forrester wrote up the requirement when OpenAI set it out. Put the two announcements side by side and you get a market where the strongest systems are handed out by application and background check instead of by price. I have never had to prove who I am to buy software. For frontier AI that is now the default.

## The takeaway

If you build on these APIs, assume the model you can actually buy sits one step behind the model that exists, and stop planning around whatever tops the benchmark charts in a given week. Watch for Google to put a date on Ultra and API access, because the lag between announcement and availability is the number I would track from here. And if you do security work at a hospital, a utility, a bank or a provincial ministry, go look at Fairwind and Trusted Access today, because you may qualify for tools nobody else can buy at any price.
